arguments.name: Volume 4 is not an abandonment of resurrection apologetics
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Volume 4's focus on theological and practical implications does not mean Habermas has given up on evidential resurrection apologetics.
premises: P1 The book has two halves: the first half treats God, miracles, and worldview, and the second half is almost no apologetics by his definition.
P2 Resurrection apologetics still appears here and there, but it is not the concentration of the volume.
P3 The series is built on the evidential case of volume 1 and the reputational/historical case of volume 2, without which volume 4 could not be done at a scholarly level.
P4 Habermas has always been a strict evidentialist and would not do subjective or presuppositionalist apologetics even if paid.

st2.quote: The second half of the book is almost no apologetics by my uh definition.

st3.quote: The resurrection argument stands on a evidences volume one, b reputations volume two.

st4.quote: You may not like my reasons, but don't say I'm not giving reasons.

st5.quote: They said, well, see, this is Gary admitting that the evidence for the resurrection is no good.

st6.quote: Resurrection apologetics is going to come up here and there, but it's not anything I concentrate on so much.

st8.quote: I've known Gary for what 16 years now, 16 years plus, and he he's always been hardcore strict evidentialism

or1.quote: The second half of the book is almost no apologetics by my uh definition.
or1.why: This is a self-referential defense of the structure of a new volume, not a restatement of a prior apologetic argument.

or2.why: It uses the four-volume series architecture itself as evidence about Habermas's intent.

or4.why: No formalization, equation, or model is added.

arguments.name: Skeptical objections are unfalsifiable and silly
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The objection that volume 4 abandons evidence is not worth answering because radical skeptics will never be satisfied.
premises: P1 If skeptics are really skeptical, no answer will make a difference; they will move to another objection or invent a new story.
P2 The objection itself is absurd because Habermas continues to give reasons and evidence.
P3 The critics ignore volumes 1 and 2, which still stand as the evidential foundation.

arguments.name: Theism and afterlife are linked
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: An evidential afterlife case is a strong argument for God because an afterlife cannot be explained by naturalism.
premises: P1 Russell's Why I Am Not a Christian treats God and the afterlife as the two things needed for theism.
P2 If there is an afterlife, one must ask why; it does not follow from any naturalism Habermas knows.
P3 An afterlife cannot come from time plus chance plus the natural world.
P4 Therefore an afterlife points to a God who is needed for it.

st5.quote: So, now you got to ask, if God raised him from the dead, why why did God raise him from the dead?

st6.quote: I think it's a strong argument, but I think it's once you have an afterlife, you've got to ask why.

arguments.name: Resurrection entails God and the deity of Christ
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: If the resurrection occurred, it entails a God who raised Jesus and links to Jesus' unique claims, including his deity.
premises: P1 If there is a resurrection, there must be a God who did it.
P2 No founder of the major world religions was reportedly raised from the dead, nor were Old Testament figures such as Moses, Daniel, or David.
P3 Jesus' leading teaching was the kingdom of God and how to enter it, and he claimed to hold the keys to it.
P4 God would not raise a false teacher from the dead, so Jesus' major teaching must be true.
P5 Jesus' ethical life and claims further support the link to his deity.

st2.quote: God doesn't wouldn't raise a heretic from the dead.

st3.quote: Moses didn't rise from the dead. Daniel didn't rise from the dead. David didn't rise from the dead.

st4.quote: If pre if he preached good e ethics and yet his major teaching the kingdom of God how to get there was false. seems to me that the major the falseness of the major rules out the truth the truth of the minor.

st5.quote: Now, why Jesus? Why not these other people? Why not the founders of any of the world major religion?

st6.quote: I think backdoor if you've got a resurrection, you could argue back to who did it.

st8.quote: Even critical scholars, Dale Allison, I mean others, uh, they think it's likely that Jesus foretold his death and resurrection ahead of time.

or1.quote: If there's a resurrection, I think there's a God.
or1.why: It is a variant of the standard resurrection-to-God inference, extended to the deity of Christ.

or2.quote: Even critical scholars, Dale Allison, I mean others, uh, they think it's likely that Jesus foretold his death and resurrection ahead of time.
or2.why: It brings critical-scholarship support for Jesus' prediction of his resurrection.

or3.quote: God doesn't wouldn't raise a heretic from the dead.
or3.why: It connects resurrection to the moral argument and God's omnibenevolence.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Risen Jesus and Future Hope, 2003; William Lane Craig, Assessing the New Testament Evidence for the Historicity of the Resurrection of Jesus, 1989
arguments.weakest_link: P4 (God would not raise a false teacher) is a theological intuition that needs defense against counterexamples.
arguments.develop_next: Show from the Gospels that Jesus' kingdom claims were central and that he staked his credibility on them.

arguments.name: Scripture is entailed by the resurrection
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Scripture is entailed by the resurrection, though further down the line than the kingdom and ethics.
premises: P1 If Jesus is Lord and was raised, his view of Scripture ought to be obeyed.
P2 Jesus' two greatest commandments concern loving God and loving others, and Scripture follows from accepting his teaching.
P3 God did not raise Jesus merely to affirm a view of the Bible, but Scripture is still entailed somewhere down the line.

arguments.name: Criteria for identifying a miracle
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: A miracle is best identified as a one-time event, performed by God, with very good evidence, serving as a sign to authenticate a message.
premises: P1 A miracle is an act of God or an invisible agent, and by Christian standards such an agent is God or God's creation.
P2 Jesus taught that miracles are signs pointing to a truth, and he tied himself to that teaching.
P3 Richard Swinburne's definition is preferable: a miracle at its best is a one-time event with very good evidence, for the purpose of evidencing a message.
P4 Repeated events under known circumstances, such as alleged levitation, are not first-rate miracles.
P5 The resurrection fits this criterion uniquely because it is unrepeatable and was predicted ahead of time.

st2.quote: a miracle is an act of God or an invisible agent.

st3.quote: I think he's right when he says if something is repeated under certain circumstances chances are that's not a miracle or if it is it's not a first rate miracle

st4.quote: I think the resurrection is a great connection between look it's never happened before.

I wouldn't mind knowing how that's done, but I don't think it's a miracle."

st8.quote: I think there's a number of them, but I think the resurrection is the key one that's puts the glue in there, the cement between the bricks, if you will.

or1.quote: I like Richard Swinsburn's definition that a miracle it's it at its best it's a one-time event where the evidence is very good.
or1.why: It adopts Swinburne's definition and applies it to the resurrection.

or2.quote: Even critical scholars, Dale Allison, I mean others, uh, they think it's likely that Jesus foretold his death and resurrection ahead of time.
or2.why: It brings the prediction of the resurrection as additional evidence beyond the event itself.

or3.why: It connects miracle criteria to Jesus' forgiveness healing as a sign.

arguments.name: Future-unknown appeals cannot defeat miracles
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The skeptical appeal to a future unknown natural explanation is self-defeating and cannot rationally defeat a miracle claim.
premises: P1 If one can always say 'maybe we will discover a natural explanation in the future,' the same move can be made against any disliked claim, such as the moon landing or planetary astronomy.
P2 The proper comeback is that maybe it will not happen in the future.
P3 Naturalism itself is often a non-empirical claim, so empiricist skeptics who use it inconsistently flunk their own epistemology.
P4 Habermas argues against seventeen or eighteen such Humean empirical comebacks in volume 2.

st1.quote: And the comeback, the right comeback is, and maybe it won't happen in the future.

st2.quote: you can say it about anything you don't like well maybe it'll be done in the future

st3.quote: In volume two, I have a lot of pages, two chapters divi devoted to David Hume.

st4.quote: If naturalism is not an empirical claim, but your epistemology requires empirical claims. Guess what? You flunked.

st5.quote: Well, maybe find an answer in the future. Oh, that's brilliant there, man.

st6.quote: you can say it about anything you don't like well maybe it'll be done in the future

st7.quote: If we're in the category of yes, no, yes, no. Then we did it.

st8.quote: one of which is it just makes induction impossible.

or1.quote: I argue against I think it's 17 or 18 of them in the second Hume chapter in in volume two.
or1.why: A variant: it inverts Hume's future-evidence move rather than restating Hume's argument.

or2.quote: What if I find out in the future we didn't go to the moon?
or2.why: Adds a systematic catalogue of 17-18 Humean empirical comebacks, but the underlying data are Hume's own examples.

or3.quote: If naturalism is not an empirical claim, but your epistemology requires empirical claims.
or3.why: Connects philosophy of science (induction, empiricism) to the miracle debate.

arguments.prior_art: David Hume, Of Miracles (An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, 1748); Habermas, The Resurrection, vol. 2 (2022)
arguments.weakest_link: P2 ('maybe it won't happen') is a bare counter-assertion that by itself does not settle the evidential question.
arguments.develop_next: Give a criterion for when a future-unknown appeal is legitimate vs. ad hoc, rather than a symmetric 'maybe it won't.'

arguments.name: Supernatural events can be linked to God rather than Satan
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: If a skeptic grants a supernatural event, linking it to God rather than Satan is reasonable because the skeptic's own worldview cannot accommodate Satan or other supernatural beings.
premises: P1 The skeptic who says 'maybe Satan did it' has already admitted supernatural beings into his theory, which he normally denies.
P2 If supernatural beings, intelligent design, fine-tuning, an afterlife, and objective ethics are granted, all five require a being fairly called God.
P3 Therefore the skeptic who grants the supernatural has sped up the case for God rather than avoided it.

st2.quote: If you have supernatural beings, if you have intelligent design, if you have fine-tuning, if you have an afterlife, if you have objective ethics, um, from, you know, out of nowhere, uh, causally, uh, I think all five of those require, uh, a being that that's fair to call him God.

st4.quote: Now, we've got about five things here that seem that they require God.

st5.quote: I don't know. Now, we've got about five things here that seem that they require God.

st6.quote: I think all five of those require, uh, a being that that's fair to call him God.

st8.quote: If intelligent design is True. That may not prove God, but it sure helps.

or1.quote: you don't allow Satan anywhere in your theory
or1.why: A variant of the standard tu quoque against naturalism, applied to the Satan objection specifically.

or2.why: No new evidence; the five items are generic theistic arguments.

or3.quote: five things here that seem that they require God
or3.why: Bundles five distinct domains (design, fine-tuning, afterlife, ethics, supernatural beings) into one lever.

arguments.weakest_link: P2 asserts all five items 'require' God without argument for any of them.
arguments.develop_next: Argue at least one of the five (e.g. objective ethics) to God rather than asserting the bundle.

arguments.name: Competing miracle claims do not match the resurrection
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Competing miracle claims from other religions or Christian traditions do not undermine the resurrection because they lack comparable evidence and often do not require God.
premises: P1 One must investigate each alleged competing miracle, and most cannot be verified even by their own adherents.
P2 Alleged levitation or anti-gravity events do not require God and are not first-rate miracles.
P3 The Quran has no verse that Muhammad did miracles, but it does have verses that Jesus did miracles.
P4 Marian apparitions such as Medjugorje or Zeitoun are contested, often involve only a handful of visionaries, and are usually within the Christian fold.
P5 The resurrection is the culmination of Jesus' unique life, teaching, predictions, and ethical influence, so it stands alone.

st6.quote: I think it's unique when it's unique with Jesus.

st7.quote: We're never going to get to the end of this because we have to investigate each one and be sure it's true.

st8.quote: you don't find this stuff outside of the uh I I mean true true cases

or1.why: A variant of the standard evidential-superiority reply to the competing-miracles objection.

or2.quote: in Medigoria the people watch the kids watch Mary. There's only a handful of them.
or2.why: Brings concrete apparition data (Medjugorje, Zeitoun) and Quranic verses into the comparison.

or3.why: Crosses comparative religion with intra-Christian polemics.

arguments.weakest_link: P5 (resurrection as unique culmination) assumes the uniqueness it needs to show.
arguments.develop_next: Give explicit, side-by-side evidential criteria and score the resurrection against two named rival miracle claims.

arguments.name: Arguments for God and from miracles work both ways

arguments.conclusion: One can argue prospectively from God to the resurrection or retrospectively from the resurrection back to God, and Scripture does both.
premises: P1 The prospective path moves from God to Jesus and his resurrection.
P2 The retrospective path begins with the unique event and asks who could have done it, then connects to arguments for God.
P3 The New Testament argues both ways, so the direction is not a problem.

arguments.name: Chapter one offers considerations, not strict proofs, for God
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Chapter one does not attempt to prove God's existence deductively but presents a theistic universe with good considerations and signs.

P3 He does not think many things can be proved apodictically; things are established by high probability.

arguments.name: Jesus claimed deity, especially in Mark 2 and Mark 14
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Jesus claimed to be deity through a multiplicity of texts, with Mark 14:61-64 being the strongest.
premises: P1 Critics who demand a verse where Jesus says 'I am God' are misguided because Jesus never used that exact phrase.
P2 In Mark 2, Jesus forgives sins and heals to show he has authority on earth to forgive sins, which the rabbis recognized as God's prerogative.
P3 In Mark 14, Jesus says 'I am,' claims to be the cloud rider, and says he will sit at the right hand of God, which the high priest calls blasphemy.
P4 Del Rosario's dissertation on Mark 2 and Mark 14 provides the best treatment of these claims and answers to objections.

st2.quote: The big one is what he says last. I will be seated on the right hand of God.

st3.quote: the high priest immediately tears his garment and says you committed blasphemy

st4.quote: in the Old Testament, only God is a cloud rider.

st5.quote: Now, some critics, Bartman's a good example, some critics will say, I I challenge you Christians. Give me one verse where Jesus says, "I am God."

st6.quote: I think the fact that he claimed to be deity or divinity is shown by a multiplicity of things.

st8.quote: First one is one we already did. the guy who comes through the roof and he says, "Son, your sins are forgiven."

or1.quote: I would take Mark 14 there to over any verse in the Gospel of John.
or1.why: A variant of the standard 'implicit Christology' argument, prioritizing Mark over John.

or2.quote: D Rosario does the whole book on Mark Mark 2 and Mark 14.
or2.why: Brings Del Rosario's dissertation as new supporting scholarship.

arguments.weakest_link: P3's cloud-rider and right-hand-seat claims depend on contested exegesis of Daniel 7 and Psalm 110.
arguments.develop_next: Lay out Del Rosario's criteria for a deity claim and rebut the 'son of man = mere human' reading explicitly.
